verdict.reasoning: She reports a cough and runny nose for “maybe five or six days ago” and describes the cough as “quite dry.”
She says the cough is “just so continuous… it’s quite dry and it’s just all day. Like, keeps me up at night as well.”
Clinician clarifies “You don't bring up any mucky phlegm or anything like that? No, no.” indicating a non‑productive cough.
She states “the coughing is giving me a sore throat… just my throat is irritated from coughing.”
She clarifies it is “not that bad when I swallow or anything,” indicating no painful swallowing.
She says “I don't feel breathless, no. I feel, you know, generally tired.”
She reports “my muscle was really hurting… Especially, like, in my arms, my legs, like, just everywhere.”

She describes “shivers even when I'm in bed… I haven't taken my temperature. So I'm not 100% sure if I had a fever, but feels like I probably did,” which is chills and subjective fever without measurement.

She notes “at the beginning… I had a little bit of diarrhea… Has it got better now… Yeah, yeah, it got better… it started at the same time as the cough started, and then it stopped,” indicating transient diarrhea now resolved.
When asked “Any pain in your chest?” she replies “No, not that either.”
She says “I don't think so… You don't feel breathless, do you? I don't feel breathless, no,” indicating no baseline shortness of breath.
She reports “No, they feel okay, actually” regarding ears and confirms no pain or discharge when asked, “No pain or discharge?”
She answers “No, no. No nausea, no vomiting” when asked about these symptoms.
She states “Well, I have type 2 diabetes.”
She says “I have quite high blood pressure.”
She reports “I take Metformin for the diabetes.”
She reports “And I take Lisinopril for the high blood pressure.”
The transcript lists metformin as a current medication but there is no explicit plan stated to continue metformin.
Lisinopril is documented as a current medication, but no explicit statement is made that the plan is to continue lisinopril.
On being asked about allergies she replies “No allergies, no.”
She notes “My dad also has type 2 diabetes.”
She states “It's just me and my partner” and confirms “Yeah. He has none of this… He's fine,” indicating a well partner at home.
She says “I am a developer.” The clinician restates “So you work in the IT field,” consistent with software developer.
She reports “I used to [smoke], but I've stopped for about six months now,” indicating ex‑smoker who quit 6 months ago.
She says she drinks “maybe two or three glasses” of wine on “like, say, three evenings a week,” matching the described pattern.

Clinician concludes “I think essentially… a bit of a viral illness… you've had a bit of a cough, bit of a runny nose, feeling quite weak and lethargic… It's been five days,” consistent with an acute viral URTI with 5–6 days of rhinorrhea, dry cough, myalgia, and subjective fever.

She has “type 2 diabetes” and states regarding her conditions, “I have it under control, and since I've started taking this medication, I've just been regularly checking that it's under control,” and she takes metformin for diabetes.

She has “quite high blood pressure” treated with lisinopril and similarly says of her conditions, “I have it under control… checking that it's under control,” implying hypertension controlled on lisinopril.
She reports the cough “is just so continuous… keeps me up at night” and that it is giving her a sore throat: “just my throat is irritated from coughing.”
The clinician advises “get some nice rest, drink plenty of fluids, keep yourself well hydrated,” which is supportive care with rest and fluids.
The clinician states “You can take regular paracetamol,” in the context of managing her viral illness with fever/chills and myalgia.
The clinician advises “maybe take a day or two off work if you can get some good bed rest, and maybe think about work early next week.”
There is counseling to reduce alcohol: “maybe something that you can maybe cut down on… Why don't you cut down to two glasses a week and then one week thereafter.”

The clinician says if not better in 2–3 days and “still feeling feverish and your cough isn't getting any better, then we may look to give you some antibiotics for your chest, which can sometimes be a common source of infection,” indicating possible future antibiotics for chest infection.

While she mentions regular checks for diabetes and hypertension, no explicit plan in this encounter is stated that she “should have routine follow-up” for these; it is implied background, not an articulated plan.
The clinician advises “If you feel like it's still any better in two to three days, it's probably worth coming back to see me again,” indicating review in 2–3 days if not improving.

They state “if your cough isn't getting any better or your breathing is getting worse, I want you to come back and see me sooner,” which covers worsening breathlessness/clinical deterioration; high fever worsening is implied in earlier context about feeling feverish.
During discussion of sputum the clinician remarks “Oh, I can hear that,” in response to her coughing, indicating an audible dry cough during the interview.
No physical examination findings or vital signs (e.g., temperature, BP, HR, chest exam) are documented anywhere in the transcript.
